newsitem.title: USA: Congress bipartisanship fades, Republicans battle.
newsitem.headline: Congress bipartisanship fades, Republicans battle.

text.p: Three months into a new U.S. congressional session, bipartisan cooperation promised in January has faded and frustrated Republicans are threatening revolt against their leaders.

While Republicans feuded in past weeks, bemused Democrats watched from the sidelines and decried the lack of progress on the major issues facing Congress -- balancing the budget, reforming the Medicare health care system, and acting on nominations to President Bill Clinton's cabinet.
After battles on everything from abortion to campaign finances, the lawmakers took a two-week cooling-off break on Friday, enabling them to get back in touch with their voters.
Democrats have accused Republicans of going on a "witch hunt" with broad investigations into the minority party's campaign finance practices.
The atmosphere was scarcely better within the Republican majority, which has seen little success on its top goals.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich, once the catalyst for change, has become the lightning rod for frustration within the Republican party. Gingrich was re-elected Speaker under an ethics cloud, formally reprimanded by the House and still has to pay a $300,000 penalty.

The Republican majority started splitting at the seams after Gingrich made the suggestion on Monday that one of their core priorities, a tax cut, might be put on hold until other budget issues were settled. Gingrich spent the rest of the week attempting to reassure the rank-and-file.

He defended his leadership, saying he had been told it was too dictatorial and decided to give members more room to make decisions. "Then I was told recently people need more direction. Then I was told they didn't quite understand the direction," he said at a news conference.
He said he had returned to his former position of using the House floor as a forum for setting direction of the party.
On Thursday night, 11 angry Republicans handed party leaders an embarrassing setback by voting with Democrats to delay funding for an investigation of alleged Democratic campaign financing abuses.
Republican leaders have had little success on their other major goals for the year.

After putting months of political energy into work for passage of a balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution, Republican leaders saw it fail by one vote. Similarly, House Republican leaders failed to muster the votes for passage of legislation to set limits on House terms.

Budget Committee leaders met with Clinton at the White House last week in an attempt to jump start negotiations, but conceded Congress will not meet the April 15 deadline to write the fiscal 1998 budget.

The only major legislation sent to the White House was a bill to release funds for international family planning programmes, a move fought by many conservative Republicans. Then the House delved into the most polarising of all issues -- abortion -- sending the Senate for vote next month a bill to ban one controversial abortion procedure.

"Rather than find areas for which there could be agreement, the Republicans chose to find areas for which there is deep disagreement, including the constitutional amendment on balancing the budget," Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle said as Congress prepared to go on a two-week recess.

Representative Joe Scarborough of Florida, one of 11 Republicans who mutinied on Thursday night on the House floor, accused the leaders of "malaise," and said they were "still shell-shocked" after Clinton won the political battle over the two government shutdowns in the last session.
"If they expect us to continue to vote with them and salute them in the future, they're going to have to do better than what they've done," he said at a news conference.
